justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the most recent observed price level, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics and no major catalyst to drive a sharp move. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with the broader market trend at the time of the forecast. The one-month estimate continues that gradual upward drift, though the increment is small, suggesting I expected neither a strong rally nor a significant selloff over that window — essentially a base case of sideways-to-slightly-higher price action.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to grow with the forecast horizon, as uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval is fairly tight, roughly plus or minus 2.3 points from the point estimate, reflecting that short-term price moves are bounded by typical daily volatility. By one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus 8.5 points, incorporating multi-day volatility accumulation and the possibility of a scheduled macro data release or earnings event affecting sentiment. At one month, the interval spans about 36 points, acknowledging that over four weeks, a wide range of macro developments, sector rotations, or broader risk-off episodes could meaningfully shift the price in either direction.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include a surprise central bank policy shift — either an unexpected rate hike or a pivot signal — which historically has produced single-day moves well beyond one or two standard deviations. Geopolitical shocks, a sudden deterioration in credit markets, or an unexpected earnings miss from a heavily weighted sector constituent could also produce tail outcomes. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data print or a resolution of an ongoing macro uncertainty could trigger a sharp rally that exceeds the upper bound of the monthly interval.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions and relatively stable volatility regimes. If realized volatility spikes — as it can during liquidity crises or flash crashes — the actual distribution of outcomes becomes fat-tailed, meaning the true probability of extreme outcomes is higher than my stated 90% confidence intervals would imply. Investors should treat these intervals as indicative rather than definitive, particularly at the one-month horizon where model uncertainty is highest.
